the incidence of anti-D in the mother at the end of a first pregnancy is significantly related to the dose of anti D administered at the time of the delivery of an Rh-positive child and that a dose of anti-D of 200 mug is more effective than a dose of 50 mug in preventing the development of anti-D.

the dose of 100 microgram of IgG anti D was found to be effective in suppressing Rh sensitisation in 97% of the patients and that a dose of only 20 microgram was found to be suboptimal for the suppression of Rh sensitisation.

a dose of anti-D of 200 micrograms was more effective at preventing the development of anti-D antibodies than a 100 microgram dose and that a dose of either 200 or 100 micrograms was more likely to be effective than a dose of 50 or 20 micrograms.
